# The Sync Heap: Delete First, Ask Questions Later

**Abstract**

Heaps (priority queues) are among the best-studied data structures in computer science. In this paper, we critically revisit the textbook assumption that in the comparison model at least one of the two standard heap operations of inserting an element and deleting the minimum must take logarithmic time.

By decoupling the deletion itself from the act of revealing the identity of the deleted element to the user, we avoid the sorting barrier and obtain a novel trade-off between the complexities of heap operations. This shows that _the logarithmic barrier is not inherently the cost of deleting the minimum but rather the information cost of immediately learning which element was deleted_. In the special case when the user inspects the heap state only constantly many times, we show that both insertions and deletions can be supported in constant amortized time. As an application, this yields a runtime improvement from O(_n_log_n_) to the optimal O(_n_) for a textbook unit-time scheduling problem.

We obtain our results by designing a new data structure, the _sync heap_, which gains speed by rearranging and compacting its operations until queries force it to synchronize and reveal its state. As a key component, we use the soft heap introduced by Chazelle as part of his minimum spanning tree algorithm. Our data structure is simple, comparison-based, and deterministic, and our results are asymptotically optimal.

### 1 Introduction

A central principle in the study of algorithms is the information-theoretic lower bound for sorting. It implies, in particular, that no comparison-based heap<sup>1</sup> data structure can support both `insert` and `delete-min` operations in sub-logarithmic time, since doing so would imply a heapsort with _o(n_log_n_) running time for an input of size _n_, contradicting the lower bound for sorting. Implicit in this argument is the assumption that deleting the minimum also reveals its identity; this assumption is rarely given much consideration, since in most heap implementations examining the minimum comes essentially for free.

In this paper, we revisit this basic assumption and find that it is precisely the act of revealing information to the user (_observing_ the heap) that drives the complexity of deletions. That is, we show a time complexity dichotomy between an `extract-min` operation that returns the deleted element and a _silent_ `delete-min` operation that does not report anything. We design an online data structure, the _sync heap_, that executes _n_ heap operations containing _d_ silent deletions and _k_ heap observations in O(_n+d_log_k_) total time.<sup>2</sup> In particular, if the user inspects the data structure relatively rarely, we show that all heap operations can be supported in constant amortized time, circumventing the sorting barrier.

<sup>1</sup> By _heap_ we refer here to the abstract data structure, not to a particular implementation; we use the term in preference to _priority queue_ because of its brevity. <sup>2</sup> We define log_x_ as log<sub>2</sub>(max{2_,x_}).

**Benjamin Aram Berendsohn** Max Planck Institute for Informatics **Egor Gorbachev** ETH Zürich **László Kozma** Dresden University of Technology

**Warmup: heap evaluation.** Let us start with a simpler motivating scenario in which the data structure is required to reveal information _only at the end_. Consider a sequence \(\mathcal{S}=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\dots,\sigma_n)\) of `insert` and `delete-min` operations given upfront as input. As usual, an operation `insert`(_x_) inserts an element _x_ with a given key into the heap, and a `delete-min` operation removes the element with the smallest key from the heap. The task is to compute the final state of the heap obtained by executing S from an empty heap. We require keys to be distinct and constant-time comparable, but otherwise place no restriction on them. The sequence S can intermix `insert` and `delete-min` operations arbitrarily, even allowing for prefixes with more `delete-min` than `insert` operations. In such cases, i.e., when executing a `delete-min` on an empty heap, we say that the individual operation is _unsuccessful_, not affecting the state of the data structure.

The final state of the heap is revealed in the form of an (unordered) list containing the inserted elements that survive all deletions, staying in the heap until the end. For example, for \(\mathcal{S}=\big(\text{\texttt{insert}}(a_2),\text{\texttt{insert}}(a_4),\text{\texttt{delete-min}},\text{\texttt{insert}}(a_3),\text{\texttt{insert}}(a_5),\text{\texttt{delete-min}},\text{\texttt{delete-min}},\text{\texttt{insert}}(a_1)\big)\), where key(_a<sub>i</sub>_)=_i_, a valid output is (_a_<sub>5</sub>_,a_<sub>1</sub>). Alternatively, we could ask to reveal the unordered list of all _deleted_ elements, which would be (_a_<sub>3</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,a_<sub>4</sub>). It is essential that the heap state is revealed only at the end. If we could match each `delete-min` to the identity of the deleted element, the sorting lower bound would apply, implying a logarithmic lower bound on the cost of operations.

We call this problem _heap evaluation_; it can be seen as a restricted mode of operation of heaps, natural in applications with limited data dependency, i.e., where intermediate operations are relevant only inasmuch as they affect the final state of the data structure. The task can of course be solved in O(_n_log_n_) time by running a standard online heap. The question we ask (and answer) in this paper is whether faster, i.e., O(_n_)-time algorithms are possible by taking advantage of the offline nature of the problem. We observe that even the easier problem of reporting the _minimum_ of the heap in the end was not known to be solvable faster than O(_n_log_n_).

The heap evaluation problem can be seen as a generalization of the _selection problem_, as follows. If the two types of operations are _separated_, i.e., if the sequence consists of _n_ `insert` operations followed by _d_ `delete-min` operations, then the task amounts to finding the _d_ smallest elements in a list of length _n_. This is a classical problem, well known to be solvable in deterministic O(_n_) time, e.g., by the celebrated _median-of-medians_ algorithm [BFP<sup>+</sup>73]. Algorithms for selection, however, do not seem applicable to the general problem when `insert` and `delete-min` operations are interleaved in more intricate ways (say, if each `delete-min` is preceded by two insertions).

It can be observed that the information-theoretic lower bound for sorting does not transfer to our problem. Indeed, since the number of different outputs is at most 2_<sup>n</sup>_ (subsets of the inserted elements), the classical argument can at best yield a lower bound of log<sub>2</sub>(2_<sup>n</sup>_)=_n_ on the decision-tree complexity of the problem. For other problems of a similar flavor, e.g., for _element distinctness_ or _longest increasing subsequence_, an \(\Omega(nlogn)\) lower bound can be shown in more restricted comparison or algebraic decision-tree models [Ben83, Fre75]. These results employ adversary arguments or invoke topological properties of the solution space. Transferring such techniques to the heap evaluation problem is ruled out by our first result: an optimal, linear-time algorithm.

**Theorem 1.1** (Heap evaluation)**.** _There is a deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, given a sequence_ S _of_ `insert` _and_ `delete-min` _operations on an initially empty heap, computes the (unordered) list of elements remaining in the heap after the execution of_ S _in_ O(|S|) _total time._

A key ingredient in our algorithm is Chazelle’s _soft heap_ [Cha00b], a relaxed heap data structure that trades accuracy for speed. The soft heap may increase the keys of a controlled fraction of elements called _corrupted elements_, and this limited corruption enables faster operations. In spite of corruption,

soft heaps allow us to recover partial information about the answer, thus reducing the problem size. Soft heaps were introduced by Chazelle as a crucial component of his minimum spanning tree algorithm [Cha00a], achieving the best known deterministic running time for the problem, an \(\alpha(n)\) (inverse-Ackermann) factor away from linear. Since then, simpler presentations of soft heaps have been developed [KTZ13, Bro21], and it has been repeatedly asked whether this seemingly powerful data structure has further applications. Applications to certain structured selection problems have previously been found [KKZZ19]. Our result provides a different, novel application of soft heaps.

The sync heap. The heap evaluation problem we discussed is a one-observation special case of the more general task of designing a heap data structure with optimal time complexity. In the following, we consider an arbitrary _online_ sequence of heap operations and assume that the user can inspect the heap at arbitrary times during execution.

Key to our results is a careful distinction between two types of operations: _modifications_ and _observations_. Standard heap interfaces often conflate modifications (e.g., deleting the minimum) with observations (e.g., learning the identity of the deleted element). The efficiency of our new data structure results from strictly separating these roles.<sup>3</sup> The modifications supported by the sync heap are the standard `insert` and `delete-min` operations. To emphasize the fact that in our setting `delete-min` does not report the deleted element, we sometimes call it a _silent_ `delete-min`. The two observations we support are `find-min` and `reveal-deletions`. The first is the standard operation of returning the element with the smallest key currently in the heap. The second operation is less common but nonetheless natural if we separate modifications and observations: it returns an unordered list of the elements deleted since the last reveal operation. (One can think of this operation as inspecting the state of the heap, but we return the _deleted_ elements instead of those remaining in the heap, because we do not want the output itself to dominate the running time.)

Existing optimal comparison-based heaps (e.g., Fibonacci heaps [FT87]) provide a guarantee of O(_n+d_log_n_) on the total running time of processing a sequence of _n_ heap operations containing _d_ `delete-min` operations. By explicitly separating modifications and observations, we arrive at a more fine-grained bound, showing that the optimal time complexity of deletions depends not on the total number of operations but rather on the number of observations. Precisely, we show the following:

**Theorem 1.2** (Sync heap)**.** _There is a data structure that can execute an online sequence of n heap operations of the form_ `insert`_, (silent)_ `delete-min`, `find-min`_, and_ `reveal-deletions` _in_ O(_n+d_log_k_) _total time, where d is the number of_ `delete-min` _operations and k is the number of_ `find-min` _and_ `reveal-deletions` _operations._

We show the bound of Theorem 1.2 to be optimal through a connection to the _multiple selection_ problem [DM81]. In fact, a more careful analysis of our sync heap matches a known entropy lower bound [DM81] that, in terms of our problem, takes into account the distribution of deletions between observations. More strongly, the lower bound holds even if no `reveal-deletions` operations are used.

If the only observation operation is a single `reveal-deletions` at the end, Theorem 1.2 recovers the time complexity of Theorem 1.1 for heap evaluation. On the other hand, if each (silent) `delete-min` is coupled with a `find-min`, Theorem 1.2 recovers the interface and amortized time complexity of standard optimal heaps. Between these two extremes, we get a smooth interpolation. To

<sup>3</sup> The name _sync heap_ is meant to evoke the mechanism whereby the data structure needs to synchronize only when the user chooses to observe its state, and can flexibly optimize work between observations.

<tbc>the best of our knowledge, the sync heap is the first data structure with such guarantees. Theorem 1.2 shows that, perhaps surprisingly, _looking at the minimum before deleting it_ carries with it an inherent cost, whereas omitting this observation makes deletions cheaper.

To achieve the result of Theorem 1.2, we build on the approach of Theorem 1.1 and efficiently bundle modifications between consecutive observations. This involves transforming a sequence of arbitrarily interleaved insertions and deletions into an equivalent sequence in which all deletions are performed consecutively. To perform several deletions efficiently, we use the recently introduced _selectable heap_ [SZ22]. Interestingly, this data structure also relies on soft heaps in one of its possible implementations.

Application and future work. We find the separation of modifications from observations and the resulting fine-grained bounds obtained via the sync heap to be of intrinsic interest, as they concern a basic data-structural question and model of computation. We highlight one algorithmic application to a classical scheduling problem called _single-machine maximum-profit unit-time scheduling_.

The standard O(_n_log_n_)-time algorithm for this problem dates back to the 1970s [Law76]. In §2.1 we show an improved linear-time algorithm as a simple application of sync heaps. The problem is covered in many classical algorithms textbooks including [CLRS09, §16.5], [Bru07, §4.4.2], [HSR08, §4.4], but no linear-time algorithm was known for it in the literature, to the best of our knowledge.

A possible future direction is to extend the model to other heap operations, such as `decrease-key` and `meld`, which appear to require new ideas. We believe that our techniques may have applications to other data structures as well.

Further related work. Heaps are among the best-studied data structures in computer science, due to their varied applications, e.g., in graph algorithms. A broad survey of heaps up to 2013 is given by Brodal [Bro13]. Classical binary heaps [Wil64] already support logarithmic-time basic operations, while optimal amortized times for all operations (including `meld` and `decrease-key`) were first attained by Fibonacci heaps [FT87]; these bounds were deamortized in strict Fibonacci heaps [BLT25]. Pairing heaps [FSST86] are a particularly elegant "bookkeeping-free" design that has influenced a line of work in "self-adjusting data structures". More recent designs include quake heaps [Cha13], hollow heaps [HKTZ17], slim and smooth heaps [HKST21, KS20], among others.

The sorting lower bound on the complexity of heap operations can be circumvented in various specialized settings. These include heaps with _integer keys_ [vEBKZZ76, Wil83, FW93, Tho04, Tho07], operation sequences exhibiting _structure_, such as spatial and/or temporal locality [Iac00, IL05, Elm06, DJ09, EFI12, HHR<sup>+</sup>24, vRR25, Rut26, HHRT26], heaps with _predictions_ [BC24], and heaps with relaxed correctness guarantees, such as allowing _approximate answers_ [TZZZ19, Dum19].

Similar in spirit to our work is [KZZ15], where an essentially tight trade-off is shown between the amortized costs of `insert`, `delete`, and `find-min`; see also [BCR96]. In particular, their _lazy binomial heap_ data structure achieves the amortized times O(1) for `insert`, O(_t_) for `delete`, and O(_n/_2<sup>_t_</sup>+log_n_) for `find-min`. Choosing _t_=log_k_ yields a total of O(_n+d_log_k+k_log_n_), where _k_ is the number of `find-min` and _d_ is the number of `delete` operations. Even though the bound resembles the one in Theorem 1.2, the result is not directly comparable to ours, as it concerns a `delete` operation (less common for heaps) that is given a pointer to the element to be deleted, rather than `delete-min`, for which the minimum crucially needs to be identified first. The techniques used in [KZZ15] are also rather different from ours.

Our heap evaluation problem can also be seen as related to the _checking_ problem, where a given offline sequence of _n_ heap operations (together with the outputs of operations) has to be verified for correctness. A linear-time algorithm is known for this task [FM99], using offline union-find<tbc>

<tbc>techniques [GT85]. If the ranks of all inserted elements are known, the algorithm of Gabow and Tarjan [GT85, §4] can also solve the "offline" heap evaluation problem of Theorem 1.1 in linear time, even identifying the element removed by each individual deletion. However, finding the ranks amounts to sorting; what makes our heap evaluation problem interesting is exactly the fact that the ranks are unknown.

**Note on independent work.** After our paper was made public, we became aware that a linear-time algorithm for unit-time scheduling was also described by Matthias Görgens in a Computer Science Stack Exchange answer cs.stackexchange.com/a/171695/50292, based on ideas similar to those in the proof of Theorem 1.1. Our work was developed independently.

## 2 Heap Evaluation

In this section, we prove the following theorem.

**Theorem 1.1** (Heap evaluation)**.** _There is a deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, given a sequence_ S _of_ `insert` _and_ `delete-min` _operations on an initially empty heap, computes the (unordered) list of elements remaining in the heap after the execution of_ S _in_ O(|S|) _total time._<sup>4</sup>

We introduce some basic notation. For a nonempty set _X_ of elements with distinct keys, let min(_X_) be the element of _X_ with the smallest key and max(_X_) be the element of _X_ with the largest key. If _H_ is a data structure storing a set of elements, let E(_H_) denote the contents of _H_. Given a set _X_ of elements and a sequence S of heap operations, let D(_X,_S) be the set of elements removed by all the `delete-min` operations while executing S on a heap _H_ initially satisfying E(_H_)=_X_. Finally, let R(_X,_S) be E(_H_) at the end of that execution. (Here, E stands for **e**elements, D stands for **d**eleted elements, and R stands for **r** remaining elements.) In particular, Theorem 1.1 asks to compute \(\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\).

As a baseline, executing S with an ordinary heap takes O(_n_log_n_) time, where _n_ is the total number of insertions in S.<sup>5</sup> Call this algorithm `TrivialHeapEval`.

The main tool in our improved algorithm is the soft heap of Chazelle [Cha00b]. Soft heaps achieve constant amortized time for both `insert` and `delete-min` operations by allowing some of the keys to be _corrupted_.

**Lemma 2.1** (Soft heap [Cha00b, KTZ13, Bro21])**.** _For every parameter_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2]\)_, there is a deterministic data structure that maintains a set of elements with comparable keys, supports the operations_ `insert` _and_ `delete-min`_, and satisfies the following properties. After every operation, the data structure may increase the keys of some elements. The_ `delete-min` _operation deletes an element whose current key is the smallest. Call an element_ corrupted _if its key was ever increased. The data structure guarantees that after every operation, the number of corrupted elements in the heap is bounded by_ \(\varepsilon\cdot I\)_, where I is the total number of insertions so far. Each operation takes amortized_ \(\mathcal{O}(log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})\) _time._

<sup>4</sup> Note that if distinct elements are allowed to have equal keys, the solution to the heap evaluation problem is not well-defined. For this reason, throughout the paper we assume that the keys of all elements are distinct. This limitation can be circumvented by a standard trick of comparing equal-key elements according to their insertion times. <sup>5</sup> We may assume that \(n\le|\mathcal{S}|\le 2n\) holds. To achieve this, we initially identify all unsuccessful `delete-min` operations in S and remove them from S in linear time.

## 6 The Sync Heap: Delete First, Ask Questions Later

To clearly distinguish an ordinary heap from a soft heap, we sometimes refer to the former as an _exact heap_. Our algorithm for Theorem 1.1 repeatedly executes one of two reduction steps. The first works when at most half of the inserted elements are deleted (i.e., \(|\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})|\le|\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})|\)); the second works when more than half of the inserted elements are deleted (i.e., \(|\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})|>|\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})|\)). One of the two steps is always applicable and reduces the problem size by a constant factor in linear time.

### Handling few deletions.

Our first algorithm replaces the exact heap in `TrivialHeapEval` with a soft heap with parameter \(\varepsilon=1/4\). We claim that if an uncorrupted element _x_ belongs to the soft heap \(\tilde{H}\) at the end of the execution, then _x_ would also belong to the exact heap after the same execution. Intuitively, increasing keys may postpone deletions of corrupted elements but cannot make uncorrupted elements survive for longer.

**Lemma 2.2.** _Suppose that a sequence_ S _of heap operations is executed on an initially empty soft heap_ \(\tilde{H}\)_. Let_ \(\tilde{X}\) _be the set of uncorrupted elements in_ \(\tilde{H}\) _at the end of the execution. Then_ \(\tilde{X}\) _is a subset of_ \(\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\).

**Proof.** Fix some \(x\in\tilde{X}\) and let _a_:=key(_x_). Execute S in parallel on a soft heap \(\tilde{H}\) and an exact heap _H_. For an element \(y\in\EuScript{E}(\tilde{H})\), let \(\widetilde{key}(y)\) denote the current key of _y_ in \(\tilde{H}\). At every point in time, let _N<sub>a</sub>_ be the current rank of _a_ in _H_, and let \(\tilde{N}_a\) be the current rank of _a_ in \(\tilde{H}\). Formally, let

\(N_a:=|\{y\in\EuScript{E}(H):key(y)\le a\}|\text{and}\tilde{N}_a:=|\{y\in\EuScript{E}(\tilde{H}):\widetilde{key}(y)\le a\}|.\)

We claim that \(\tilde{N}_a\le N_a\) holds at all times. Initially, both values are equal to zero. Upon an insertion, both change by the same amount. Key corruptions can only reduce \(\tilde{N}_a\). Upon a deletion, each of the two values is decremented by 1 if and only if the respective value is strictly positive. Thus, \(\tilde{N}_a\le N_a\) is maintained.

Now suppose that \(x\notin\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\). Consider the operation that deletes _x_ from _H_. Right after this operation, _N<sub>a</sub>_=0 since _x_ was the element with the smallest key in _H_ and all keys in _H_ are distinct. Consequently, \(\tilde{N}_a=0\), so either \(x\notin\EuScript{E}(\tilde{H})\) or _x_ is corrupted. This contradicts the fact that _x_ belongs to \(\tilde{X}\), finishing the proof.

We now use Lemma 2.2 to reduce the problem size if there are _few deletions_. Indeed, after executing S on a soft heap \(\tilde{H}\), we may add the set _U_ of uncorrupted elements in \(\tilde{H}\) to the answer (i.e., the set of remaining elements), remove the insertions of these elements from S, and recursively solve the problem for the new sequence \(\mathcal{S}'\). Since clearly \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})=\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S}')\), we have \(\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})=\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S}')\cup U\), and we have reduced the problem from S to \(\mathcal{S}'\). Note that removing the insertions corresponding to the set _U_ can be done with simple bookkeeping in linear time.

Let _n_ be the number of insertions. With the error parameter \(\varepsilon=1/4\), at most _n/_4 elements remaining in the soft heap at the end are corrupted. If the number of deletions is at most _n/_2, then at least _n/_2 elements are still present in \(\tilde{H}\) at the end of S, and at least _n/_4 of them are uncorrupted. Recall that \(n\le|\mathcal{S}|\le 2n\), so we have reduced the problem size by a constant factor. Next, we discuss how to handle the case with more than _n/_2 deletions.

### Handling many deletions.

The above algorithm works by maintaining an approximation of \(\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\) in a soft heap. The idea for the remaining case is simple and in a sense "dual" to the first case: maintain an approximation of \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\). We do so by scanning S backwards, using a max-heap instead of a min-heap. Intuitively, every `delete-min` creates a deletion "slot", while every `insert` provides a candidate for one of the currently open slots. If there are more candidates than slots, the largest<tbc>

candidate will survive the processed suffix. Therefore, such a maximum candidate can be discarded. The pseudocode for this algorithm, `ReverseHeapEval`, is given in Algorithm 1. Since the algorithm is slightly more complex than the previous one, we first analyze it with an exact heap.

`ReverseHeapEval(S) begin` `2` \(H\leftarrow\mathtt{MaxHeap}()\) `3` \(\delta\leftarrow 0\) _// Number of deletion slots in the processed suffix_ `4` **for** \(\sigma\in\mathtt{reversed}(\mathcal{S})\) **do** `5` **if** \(\sigma=\mathtt{insert}(x)\) **then** `6` _H._`insert`(_x_) `7` **if** \(|H|>\delta\) **then** `8` _H._`delete-max`() `9` **else if** \(\sigma=\mathtt{delete-min}\) **then** `10` \(\delta\leftarrow\delta+1\) `11 return E(_H_)` `Algorithm 1` A heap-based algorithm for computing \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\). The algorithm reverses the timeline and maintains the set of deleted elements.

`Example.` Consider the sequence \(\mathcal{S}=\big(\mathtt{insert}(a_2),\mathtt{insert}(a_4),\mathtt{delete-min},\mathtt{insert}(a_3),\mathtt{insert}(a_5),\mathtt{delete-min},\mathtt{delete-min},\mathtt{insert}(a_1)\big)\) from §1, where key(_a<sub>i</sub>_)=_i_. Starting with an empty max- heap _H_ and \(\delta=0\), `ReverseHeapEval` scans the sequence from right to left. The following table shows the state after each step; the last column records the element discarded when \(|H|>\delta\).

Thus, `ReverseHeapEval` returns \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})=\{a_2,a_3,a_4\}\), while _a_<sub>1</sub> and _a_<sub>5</sub> survive the original sequence.

**Lemma 2.3. `ReverseHeapEval`**, _when implemented with an exact max-heap, computes_ \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\).

**Proof.** We prove by induction over the suffixes T of S that after `ReverseHeapEval` processes T , the invariant \(\mathcal{E}(H)=\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{T})\) holds. Observe that \(\delta\) is the number of `delete-min` operations in T . The invariant is trivial for an empty suffix. Now suppose that the invariant holds for a suffix T , and let \(\sigma\) be the operation immediately preceding T in the original order. If \(\sigma=\mathtt{delete-min}\), then \(\sigma\) is unsuccessful in a forward execution of \(\sigma\mathcal{T}\) from an empty heap. Thus, prepending \(\sigma\) to T does not change the deleted set.

Now suppose that \(\sigma=\mathtt{insert}(x)\). A forward execution of \(\sigma\mathcal{T}\) from an empty heap is equivalent to a forward execution of T from a heap initially containing only _x_. Compare forward executions of T starting from \(\varnothing\) (heap \(F_\varnothing\)) and from {_x_} (heap _F<sub>x</sub>_) in parallel. Observe that at all times either

the heaps are identical or _F<sub>x</sub>_ contains all the elements from \(F_\emptyset\) together with one extra element _y_, where initially _y=x_. Insertions preserve this property. If \(F_\emptyset\) deletes _z_, then _F<sub>x</sub>_ deletes min{_y,z_}, leaving max{_y,z_} as its new extra element. If \(F_\emptyset\) encounters an unsuccessful deletion, _F<sub>x</sub>_ deletes its extra element, and after that the two executions are identical.

Consider the state of _H_ in `ReverseHeapEval` after processing T , before processing \(\sigma\), and recall that \(\EuScript{E}(H)=\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\mathcal{T})\) by the induction hypothesis. If \(|H|<\delta\), then an unsuccessful deletion occurs in the forward execution of T (since \(\delta\) counts all deletions while |_H_| only counts the successful ones). Therefore, both \(F_\emptyset\) and _F<sub>x</sub>_ end in the same state. Consequently, \(\EuScript{E}(H)\cup\{x\}=\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\sigma\mathcal{T})\). Note that the check \(|H|>\delta\) in Algorithm 1, line 7 fails in this case, so _x_ gets correctly inserted into _H_.

Otherwise, if \(|H|=\delta\), every deletion in \(F_\emptyset\) is successful, and the extra element of _F<sub>x</sub>_ at the end of execution is \(max(\EuScript{E}(H)\cup\{x\})\) because every deletion replaces the current extra element _y_ with max{_y,z_}. Thus, the deleted set is \((\EuScript{E}(H)\cup\{x\})\backslash\{max(\EuScript{E}(H)\cup\{x\})\}\). Observe that the check in Algorithm 1, line 7 succeeds in this case, so the algorithm is again correct.

The invariant therefore holds for every suffix. Taking T =S, `ReverseHeapEval` returns \(\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S})\) as claimed.

Adapting Lemma 2.2, after running `ReverseHeapEval` with a soft max-heap \(\tilde{H}\) instead of an exact heap, the set \(\tilde{X}\) of uncorrupted elements in \(\tilde{H}\) is a subset of \(\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S})\).<sup>6</sup> We can use this information to reduce the problem size. Simply removing all insertions of elements \(x\in\tilde{X}\) would not work; we also need to remove the corresponding `delete-min` operations. Identifying the precise deletion that removes each element, however, would reintroduce the sorting barrier. The following lemma shows that it is sufficient to remove the first `delete-min` after the insertion of _x_.

**Lemma 2.4.** _Let x be an element of_ \(\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S})\)_, and let_ \(\sigma\) _be the first_ `delete-min` _operation of_ S _after the insertion of x. Let_ \(\mathcal{S}'\) _be the sequence of operations obtained by removing_ `insert`(_x_) _and_ \(\sigma\) _from_ S_. Then_ \(\mathcal{R}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S})=\mathcal{R}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S}')\).

**Proof.** Consider two initially empty exact heaps _H_ and \(H'\). Run the first heap on S and the second one on \(\mathcal{S}'\) in parallel. (When one of the two omitted operations occurs, the second heap does nothing while the first one executes the operation.) Let _y_ be the element that \(\sigma\) deletes in _H_. Since _x_ has not been deleted yet, we have \(key(y)\le key(x)\).

If _y=x_, the claim is immediate. Otherwise, we prove that until _H_ deletes _x_, the two heaps differ only in that _H_ contains _x_ while \(H'\) contains some element _z_ with \(key(z)\le key(x)\).

Recall that \(key(y)\le key(x)\), so the property indeed holds immediately after \(\sigma\). Insertions clearly preserve this property, as do deletions in which both heaps delete the same element. The only other case is where \(H'\) deletes _z_ while _H_ deletes some \(z'\neq x\) with \(key(z')<key(x)\), in which case \(z'\) becomes the new _z_.

Finally, when the first heap deletes _x_, the second heap must delete _z_ (since all other elements are common), and from this moment on the heaps remain identical. Hence, at the end of the execution we have \(\EuScript{E}(H)=\EuScript{E}(H')\).

Lemma 2.4 allows us to remove a single element of \(\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S})\). If a subset _Z_ of \(\EuScript{D}(\emptyset,\mathcal{S})\) needs to be removed, the argument can be applied repeatedly. Algorithmically, this can be implemented in O(|S|) time by running a linear scan with a stack over S and matching each deletion with the last unmatched insertion from _Z_.

<sup>6</sup> In a soft max-heap, keys of corrupted elements decrease rather than increase.

Let us summarize the entire step of handling _many deletions_. Suppose the operation sequence S with _n_ insertions contains more than _n/_2 successful deletions, and suppose we execute `ReverseHeapEval(S)` with a soft max-heap with error parameter \(\varepsilon=1/4\). Then, at the end of the execution, the soft heap contains at least _n/_4 uncorrupted elements, all of which belong to \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\). By the previous discussion, we can remove the insertions of these elements, together with their corresponding deletions, in linear time, reducing the problem from S to \(\mathcal{S}'\), thereby reducing the problem size by a constant factor.

The heap evaluation algorithm. We can now state the complete linear-time heap evaluation procedure (Algorithm 2). The correctness of the algorithm follows from the discussion above. Note that every iteration of the while-loop takes O(_n_) time, and after each iteration, _n_ decreases by a factor of at least 4/3. Summing the geometric series yields O(_n_) total time, proving Theorem 1.1.

### 2.1 Maximum-Profit Unit-Time Scheduling

As a corollary of Theorem 1.1, we give a linear-time algorithm for the single-machine _maximum- profit unit-time scheduling_ (mputs) problem. In this problem, we have _n_ unit-time jobs released at time 0, each job _j_ with an integer due date _d<sub>j</sub>_ and a nonnegative profit _w<sub>j</sub>_. The task is to schedule the execution of the jobs on a single machine, without overlap, maximizing the sum of profits of jobs completed by their due dates.<sup>7</sup> In the standard scheduling notation, this problem is \(1|p_j=1|\sum_jw_jU_j\). We show the following result.

**Theorem 2.5.** _The mputs problem with n jobs can be solved in_ O(_n_) _time._

The problem appears in many classical textbooks on algorithms and scheduling with O(_n_log_n_)- time solutions; see [CLRS09, §16.5], [Bru07, §4.4.2], [HSR08, §4.4]. The following algorithm, originally due to Lawler [Law76], correctly solves the problem in O(_n_log_n_) time:

Cap all due dates by _n_ and process the jobs in nondecreasing order of their due dates. Maintain a min-heap _H_, initially empty. When job _j_ is processed, insert _j_ into _H_. If the number of jobs stored in _H_ is greater than _d<sub>j</sub>_, remove the minimum-profit job from _H_. At the end of the algorithm, the jobs remaining in _H_ are a maximum-profit feasible set of jobs. Furthermore, ordering the jobs in _H_ by nondecreasing due date gives a valid execution schedule.

Note that processing the jobs by their due dates does not imply a sorting bottleneck, as these values are integers between 1 and _n_; the superlinear running time is only due to the operations on heap _H_, which stores jobs with their profit as the key. Lawler’s algorithm is, in fact, similar to `ReverseHeapEval` (Algorithm 1) when implemented with an exact heap, and can be seen to solve an instance of the heap evaluation problem.

We use this observation to speed up the algorithm, as follows. Simulate the steps of the algorithm, but instead of carrying out the heap operations `insert` and `delete-min` on _H_ in real time, record them as a sequence S. Notice that the operations do not depend on the outcomes of past operations, only on the job due dates and on the number of elements currently in the heap, which we can simulate with a counter. Running the simulation clearly takes O(_n_) time. Finally, after obtaining the heap operation sequence S of length at most 2_n_, we use Theorem 1.1 to evaluate the final state of the heap in O(_n_) time. This implies Theorem 2.5.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first linear-time algorithm in the literature for mputs with arbitrary comparable profits and integer due dates, without assuming that the profits are given in sorted order. We observe that the single-machine assumption is without loss of generality: the variant with _m_ machines is equivalent to the problem with one machine and processing time 1_/m_ for each job.

## 3 The Sync Heap

In this section, we turn the offline algorithm of §2 into an online data structure we call the _sync heap_. We support operations `insert`, silent `delete-min`, `find-min`, and `reveal-deletions`. As before, we call the first two operations _modifications_ and the other two _observations_. The silent `delete-min` removes the current minimum without revealing it. The operation `reveal-deletions` returns, in arbitrary order, all elements deleted by `delete-min` operations since the last `reveal-deletions` (or since the beginning of the execution if this is the first call of `reveal-deletions`). We analyze the optimal time complexity in terms of the total number _n_ of operations and the number _k_ of observations (`find-min` and `reveal-deletions`). Building on the results of §2, we prove the following theorem.

**Theorem 3.1.** _There is a deterministic data structure, the sync heap, that supports the operations_ `insert`, `find-min`, and `reveal-deletions` in constant amortized time and silent `delete-min` operations in_ O(log_k_) _amortized time, where k is the number of_ `find-min` and `reveal-deletions` _operations up to the current moment._

Before we prove Theorem 3.1, we review an important data structure called the _selectable heap_ that we use as a component. Selectable heaps augment regular heaps with batched deletions which are executed more efficiently than individual ones.

**Lemma 3.2** (Selectable heap \[SZ22\])**.** _There is a deterministic heap that supports_ `insert` _and_ `find-min` _operations in constant amortized time and can delete and return the_ \(\ell\) _smallest elements from the heap in_ \(\mathcal{O}(\ell log\frac{m}{\ell})\) _amortized time for an arbitrary_ \(\ell\le m\)_. Here m denotes the current size of the heap._

As will be clear from the proof below, sync heaps can be seen as a generalization of selectable heaps: while selectable heaps allow multiple deletions to be processed in one batch, sync heaps allow batching an arbitrary sequence of interleaved insertions and deletions in the same time complexity.<sup>8</sup>

**Proof of Theorem 3.1.** Maintain a selectable heap \(\hat{H}\), initially empty. Between consecutive observations, we do not execute `insert` and silent `delete-min` operations on \(\hat{H}\) explicitly but rather buffer them and process them in a batch when the next observation occurs. (To simplify presentation, we regard initialization as an initial dummy observation.) Thus, throughout the execution, \(\hat{H}\) represents the state of the heap at the last observation.

Suppose an observation occurs, and let S be the buffered sequence of operations since the last observation. Let \(X:=\EuScript{E}(\hat{H})\) be the state at the previous observation. First, in O(|S|) time we remove from S all deletions that would be unsuccessful if S were executed from state _X_. Let \(\delta\) be the number of deletions that remain. By construction, all of them are successful when S is executed from _X_.

Now run the heap evaluation algorithm of Theorem 1.1 on S to compute \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\) and \(\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\). As we show later, the elements deleted when S is executed from _X_ are precisely the \(\delta\) smallest elements of \(X\cup\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\). Accordingly, to synchronize \(\hat{H}\), we perform three steps: (1) insert all elements of \(\mathcal{D}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\) into \(\hat{H}\); (2) delete the \(\delta\) smallest elements from \(\hat{H}\) (denote the returned set by \(\Delta\)); (3) insert all elements of \(\mathcal{R}(\varnothing,\mathcal{S})\) into \(\hat{H}\). The second step is executed using the selectable heap’s batch-deletion operations.

After synchronization, if the current observation is a `find-min`, simply query \(\hat{H}\) for the minimum element. If instead the current observation is a `reveal-deletions`, return the union of all computed sets \(\Delta\) since the last `reveal-deletions` operation.

The time complexity of Theorem 3.1 is optimal due to an information-theoretic lower bound. The lower bound holds even without `reveal-deletions` operations. If all insertions happen before the first `delete-min`, the problem becomes the _multiple selection problem_: given an array of size _N_, compute the elements of (zero-based) ranks _p_1_,p_2_,...,pk_, where _pi_ is the number of (silent) `delete-min` operations before the _i_-th `find-min` query. It is known [DM81, Theorem 1] that solving the multiple selection problem requires \(\Omega\left(N+\sum_{i=1}^k(p_i-p_{i-1})log\left(\frac{N}{p_i-p_{i-1}}\right)\right)\) comparisons, where _p_0=-1. Informally, Dobkin and Munro show [DM81, Theorem 1] that computing elements of ranks _p_1_,p_2_,...,pk_ is sufficient to break the array elements into _k_+1 subarrays according to the gaps between the ranks. Sorting the whole array can now be reduced to sorting each individual subarray in \(\mathcal{O}(\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}(p_i-p_{i-1})log(p_i-p_{i-1}))\) total time, where _p__k_+1=_N_. Hence, the sorting lower bound \(\Omega(NlogN)\) implies the multiple selection lower bound. This bound exactly matches the time complexity of our algorithm (1) up to a constant factor.
